title: 2 Kings 23:21–30
context: Josiah keeps an unprecedented Passover and removes remaining idolatry; the narrator praises him above all kings, yet explains that the LORD’s wrath over Manasseh’s provocation still stands. Josiah dies at Megiddo when he goes out against Pharaoh Necoh. The Hebrew preposition in 23:29, rendered “against” by WEB, is understood by some interpreters to mean Necoh went to aid the Assyrian king.

verses.text: The king commanded all the people, saying, “Keep the Passover to the LORD your God, as it is written in this book of the covenant.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king commands, “Keep the Passover to the LORD your God, as it is written in this book of the covenant.” Arminian readers see worship renewed in obedience to the recovered word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Passover restored according to Scripture. The command shows that reform included positive worship, not only the removal of idols.

verses.text: Surely there was not kept such a Passover from the days of the judges who judged Israel, nor in all the days of the kings of Israel, nor of the kings of Judah;
verses.arminianNotes: No such Passover had been kept since the days of the judges. Arminian readers see a remarkable return to covenant worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the uniqueness of this celebration. 2 Chronicles 35:1–19 gives a fuller account, which interpreters read alongside this summary.

verses.text: but in the eighteenth year of King Josiah, this Passover was kept to the LORD in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: “… in the eighteenth year of King Josiah, this Passover was kept to the LORD in Jerusalem.” Arminian readers see the speed with which reform followed the discovery of the book.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Passover celebrated in the same year. The timing shows how quickly the word led to renewed worship.

verses.text: Moreover, Josiah removed those who had familiar spirits, the wizards, and the teraphim, and the idols, and all the abominations that were seen in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem, that he might confirm the words of the law which were written in the book that Hilkiah the priest found in the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Josiah removes mediums, wizards, teraphim (household idols), and other abominations “that he might confirm the words of the law.” Arminian readers see thorough obedience to God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reform completed according to the book Hilkiah found. The verse connects every action back to the authority of Scripture.

verses.text: There was no king like him before him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses; and there was none like him who arose after him.
verses.arminianNotes: “There was no king like him before him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart.” Arminian readers see Josiah’s exceptional devotion commended.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the highest praise given to Josiah. 2 Kings 18:5 offers similar praise for Hezekiah, and interpreters note that Hezekiah is praised for trusting the LORD while Josiah is praised for turning to him according to the law.

verses.text: Notwithstanding, the LORD didn’t turn from the fierceness of his great wrath, with which his anger burned against Judah, because of all the provocation with which Manasseh had provoked him.
verses.arminianNotes: “Notwithstanding, the LORD didn’t turn from the fierceness of his great wrath … because of all the provocation with which Manasseh had provoked him.” Arminian readers see the narrator’s explanation for judgment continuing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrator’s explanation of why judgment still came. This verse is shared ground: Josiah’s reform was genuine, yet the accumulated sin of Manasseh’s era still brought exile.

verses.text: The LORD said, “I will also remove Judah out of my sight, as I have removed Israel; and I will cast off this city which I have chosen, even Jerusalem, and the house of which I said, ‘My name shall be there.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I will also remove Judah out of my sight, as I have removed Israel.” Arminian readers see the sobering certainty of judgment after long rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s word of judgment on Jerusalem and the temple. The verse echoes 21:13–14, framing the exile as God’s response to Judah’s history.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Josiah, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Josiah’s acts are recorded in the chronicles of the kings of Judah. Arminian readers see the closing formula honoring a faithful reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrator pointing to fuller records. The formula places Josiah’s reign among the kings of Judah before recounting his death.

verses.text: In his days Pharaoh Necoh king of Egypt went up against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates; and King Josiah went against him, but Pharaoh Necoh killed him at Megiddo when he saw him.
verses.arminianNotes: Pharaoh Necoh goes up toward the Euphrates, Josiah goes against him, and “Pharaoh Necoh killed him at Megiddo.” Arminian readers report the death as the text gives it, without supplying a hidden sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the brevity of the account. 2 Chronicles 35:20–24 gives a fuller narrative, and interpreters in this tradition read it with care rather than adding reasons Kings does not state.

verses.text: His servants carried him dead in a chariot from Megiddo, brought him to Jerusalem, and buried him in his own tomb. The people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah, and anointed him, and made him king in his father’s place.
verses.arminianNotes: His servants carry him dead from Megiddo to Jerusalem, and the people anoint Jehoahaz. Arminian readers see the grief of Josiah’s death and the people’s attempt to maintain stability.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the end of a faithful reign and the beginning of decline. The people’s choice of Jehoahaz begins the final chapter of Judah’s kings.
